opus-5.5.text:
Well, my honest first reaction was that a gold medal at the IMO is impressive, but it isn't the same thing as research. Olympiad problems are hard, but they're designed to be solved. Someone already knows the answer, the problem is carefully posed, and there's a guarantee that a clever high-school student can crack it in a few hours with a fairly standard toolkit. Research is different. You often don't know whether the statement you're trying to prove is even true. You have to decide which questions are worth asking, you work on something for weeks or months, and most of your ideas fail.

So I didn't take the IMO result as proof that these models could do research. I took it as a signal that the raw reasoning ability was getting strong enough that it was worth testing directly. The question for me was: can it actually help on a problem that nobody has solved?

So I tried it on an open problem in my own area, optimization, a question about the convergence behavior of accelerated gradient methods that people had been stuck on for a while. I didn't just ask it once and get a finished proof. It was much more of a back-and-forth. The model would propose arguments, and a lot of them were wrong, sometimes confidently wrong. My job was to act as the filter: spot the flawed steps, recognize when an idea was actually promising, and push it in that direction. Over a number of sessions, it surfaced ideas I hadn't considered, and some of them turned out to be the key pieces.

My assessment, then, is somewhere in the middle. The IMO performance told me the model had real mathematical skill, not just pattern-matching on textbook problems. But on its own, it isn't yet a research mathematician. It doesn't reliably know when it's right, and it lacks the judgment about what matters. Paired with an expert who can verify and steer, though, it's already a genuinely useful collaborator. It explores the space of ideas very quickly, and that changes how I think about doing math.

r001.rationale: It says Olympiad problems are designed to be solved in a few hours by a clever high-school student.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes research from Olympiad problems by saying that the Olympiad answer is already known.

r003.rationale: It says Ryu tested the model on an open problem in his area of optimization, but does not say the problem was one of his own research problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that the Olympiad result and mathematical research are related but quite different things, and I tried to be careful not to collapse them.

The IMO gold was genuinely impressive. Those problems are hard, the solutions are long and have to be rigorous end to end, and the model produced them in natural language under something like the real time constraint. A few years ago I would not have predicted that. So I don't want to downplay it.

But Olympiad problems are designed to be solvable. Someone has already verified there's a clean answer reachable in a few hours with known techniques. Research isn't like that. In research you don't know whether the statement is even true, you don't know which tools apply, and most of the work is figuring out what the right question is. The IMO tells you the model can execute a difficult, well-posed problem. It tells you much less about whether it can find a problem worth solving.

So what I actually did was give it problems from my own area, convex optimization, where I knew the landscape. Things that were open, or at least not written down anywhere. And the experience was mixed in an interesting way. Left alone, it often went in circles or confidently asserted things that were false. But when I steered it, when I said "this direction is wrong, try reasoning about this quantity instead," it could carry out the hard technical steps remarkably well, sometimes faster than I could. In one case it contributed a key piece to an argument that became a real result.

So my assessment was something like: the IMO showed the proving capability is there. What's not yet there is the judgment about where to point it. For now the productive mode is a collaboration where the human provides the direction and taste, and the model provides a lot of the technical horsepower. Whether that gap closes is the question I find most interesting, and I honestly don't know the answer.

astra-6.text:
I took it as a very impressive demonstration of mathematical problem-solving, but not yet a demonstration that it could do mathematical research autonomously. An Olympiad problem is difficult, but it’s also carefully constructed: you know the question, you know a solution exists, and you have a fairly clear standard for success.

In research, a lot of the work is figuring out what question to ask. Is the statement you’re trying to prove even true? If it’s false, is there a useful counterexample? If you change the assumptions, does that lead somewhere interesting? And then there’s judging whether the result matters.

So the performance made me more optimistic about these systems contributing to research. But I would distinguish being able to solve a very hard, well-defined problem from being able to navigate an open-ended research project. The natural next step is to test them on research questions where we don’t already know the answer.

r001.rationale: The response calls Olympiad problems carefully constructed and well-defined, but does not say their solutions are relatively short or that contestants must solve them within a few hours.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes Olympiad problems from research by saying a solution is known to exist for an Olympiad problem, unlike open-ended research questions.

r003.rationale: It proposes testing systems on research questions with unknown answers, but does not specifically propose using Ernest Ryu’s own research problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between solving an exceptionally hard problem and doing mathematical research. The Olympiad result is impressive evidence of mathematical problem-solving ability. But in a competition, someone has already chosen the question, and you know there’s a solution you’re supposed to find.

In research, you often don’t know whether your conjecture is true, whether your approach will lead anywhere, or even whether you’re asking the right question. You have to make those judgments as you go. So I’d take the performance as a strong sign of progress on an important part of research, but I wouldn’t infer research ability from that result alone. For that, I’d want to see it work on genuinely open problems and produce new mathematics that survives careful scrutiny.
